problem: The text says one node can read another node's memory over the LAN. In a cluster each node is an independent computer with its own private memory; nodes exchange data by message passing, not by reading each other's RAM. Direct remote memory access only exists with special interconnects (RDMA/SCI) and is not the general cluster model.
fix: Each node keeps its own memory. Pieces of the same job exchange data by passing messages over the LAN, which is fast enough for the pieces to work together while they run. Some clusters add special interconnects that allow one node to reach another node's memory directly, but a plain LAN does not.

problem: The chain mainframe → cluster → grid → utility → cloud is presented as the order of events. As a logical build-up it is fine, but as history it is loose: selling computing by the meter was already discussed in the mainframe time-sharing era, well before grids appeared, so a student may read the arrows as dates.
fix: Add one sentence: this is the order in which the ideas build on each other, not a strict timeline; metered charging was talked about in the mainframe years, and grids came later as a way to reach capacity outside one owner's walls.

problem: Step 8 adds power, cooling and staff to the bought option, but step 4 charges only ₹30 per server-hour for renting. The comparison silently assumes the rent already covers power, cooling and staff, and also that the bought servers need no extra staff during the peak days. The arithmetic is correct; the assumption is unstated.
fix: Add a line after step 4: the ₹30 per server-hour rent is taken to include power, cooling and staff, so the rented side carries no separate running cost; the bought side pays ₹3,00,000 per month on top of the purchase price.
